(Illustration by Thomas Gaulkin; Photo (modified) by Dominique Jacovides / Abaca / Alamy) Copy link Linked copied Email Facebook Bluesky Twitter LinkedIn WhatsApp Reddit Spread Listen to this article: When French President Emmanuel Macron introduced the concept of forward deterrence during his March 2 speech on France’s nuclear policy at the Île Longue nuclear submarine base, many European governments enthusiastically endorsed it. Since Russia’s February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Europeans have been increasingly concerned about deterring Russian aggression. At the same time, the Trump administration’s unpredictability and disengagement from European security undermine the value of NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. Against this backdrop, Macron’s proposal for a strengthened European nuclear deterrent seemed to square several circles for non-nuclear-weapon NATO members: It aims to bring French nuclear weapons closer into the European security equation, without angering Washington. And Macron emphasized that his initiative complements—rather than competes with—NATO’s nuclear-sharing arrangements, which many Europeans want to leave intact as long as possible. Four months on, things increasingly turn out not to be so simple. Implementation of the initiative is uneven, its level of ambition remains unclear, and questions remain around compatibility with the US nuclear extended deterrent. To address these problems, France’s non-nuclear partners should increase coordination among themselves on nuclear issues, rather than engage Paris on a one-to-one basis only. Earlier and better harmonization of their own positions would make it easier for them to pursue their own interests vis-à-vis Paris effectively. Increased coordination would also facilitate better alignment of the French concept of forward deterrence with NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. An uneven playing field. Nine partners have now expressed varying degrees of interest in participating in the French initiative on forward deterrence, which can involve participating in French nuclear exercises to practice support for nuclear-strike missions and, potentially, the temporary deployment of French nuclear-capable aircraft to bases on the territory of other participating countries. During crises or conflicts, dispersing French nuclear capabilities could help to improve their survivability and, therefore, strengthen deterrence. Different from NATO nuclear sharing , there would be no formal security guarantee, no permanent deployment of nuclear assets to third countries, and no joint decision-making on nuclear policies. During his address, President Macron mentioned Belgium, Denmark, Germany, Greece, Poland, the Netherlands, and Sweden as non-nuclear partners. Since then, Norway and France signed the Narvik agreement on bilateral defense relations , which includes Oslo joining the French initiative on European nuclear deterrence, bringing the number of non-nuclear partners to eight. The other European nuclear-weapon state, the United Kingdom, has a long-standing cooperation with France on nuclear deterrence. In addition, Finland has expressed an interest in joining the initiative and, on June 17, changed a law to make it legal to deploy nuclear weapons on its territory during a crisis or conflict. And in April, Czech President Andrej ‌Babis also expressed interest in discussing involvement in forward deterrence, but it remains unclear whether additional steps have been taken since. To avoid the perception of competing with NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group, which brings together all 32 NATO states except France, Paris will engage its nuclear partners bilaterally. Coordination of these dialogues is likely to impose a large burden on the French bureaucracy. But it also conveniently situates Paris at the center of a web of deterrence dialogues, making it easier to tailor the terms and conditions of partnerships to its liking. From the perspective of France’s partners, this arrangement of separate dialogues is less advantageous. Each partner will bring specific interests to the table, influenced by geography, domestic politics, strategic culture, and history. Two things unite them: the hope that participation in forward deterrence will improve their security, and a desire to shape French nuclear policies in ways that meet their specific interests. These core interests have always been two drivers behind the non-nuclear Allies’ involvement in NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. They hope that, in nuclear consultation, “ the gap between the interests of the nuclear power as security provider and nonnuclear protégés as security beneficiaries ” could be bridged. As a result, non-nuclear allies want their nuclear-armed allies to inform and consult them on nuclear policies, including on the existential question of when, where, and how nuclear weapons will be used. Such nuclear consultations have often been difficult and occasionally controversial in NATO, and France’s new nuclear partners will not just want to be consumers of what Paris has to offer but will bring their own demands to the table. Better alignment of their policies would make it easier to ensure that dialogue is a true two-way street. Such coordination would be easier if France’s partners were to approach Paris from a level playing field. However, at least for now, there appear to be different categories of nuclear partners. In his speech, Macron singled out the United Kingdom as “a major partner” and Germany as “crucial partners [sic].” London and Berlin will converse with Paris through newly established nuclear steering groups, which have already met at senior political levels. On the same day of announcing the French initiative, President Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz published a joint declaration , which is “based on the shared understanding that the nuclear dimension of deterrence remains a cornerstone of European security.” Nuclear cooperation between the two NATO nuclear weapon states—France and the United Kingdom—is long-standing, and both have recently intensified it with agreement on the Northwood Declaration . Sweden is the third country that has engaged Paris through a nuclear steering group . Two months after Macron’s speech, Paris and Stockholm signed a multi-billion-euro defense deal. President Macron placed the agreement squarely in the context of the closer strategic partnership that led to Sweden’s participation in the French initiative on forward deterrence. On July 10, France and Poland held their first Nuclear Steering Group meeting in Paris “to discuss European security issues.” Senior officials from defense and foreign ministries agreed on a “joint roadmap.” Paris may want to establish Nuclear Steering Groups with all nine current nuclear partners. But given the depth and range of cooperation under the forward deterrence initiative, it is likely to vary from country to country. A one-way street on nuclear policy? Non-nuclear allies participate in extended deterrence arrangements for two main reasons: They hope that positive security guarantees from the nuclear-armed ally will avert attacks against them. And they use consultations under these arrangements to influence the nuclear policies and force postures of the nuclear ally. This has been true under NATO’s nuclear consultative mechanisms and will also drive involvement of France’s partners in nuclear deterrence arrangements. But Paris has historically been opposed to the concept of joint nuclear discussions and decision-making. Preserving national autonomy was, after all, the main reason why Paris decided not to join NATO’s Nuclear Planning Group when it was set up in 1966. During his Île Longue speech, Macron repeated the “four noes” that are at the core of French nuclear autonomy: No joint decision on nuclear use, no joint planning, no sharing of the definition of French vital interests, no nuclear guarantee “in the strict sense of the term.” These limits suggest that Paris expects its partners to adapt to French traditional nuclear thinking with little room for give-and-take. It therefore remains unclear whether and to what extent France’s partners will be able to influence Paris to take their national security interests into account. A brochure published by the French Ministry of Defense after Macron’s speech repeats that “France’s nuclear deterrent is not subject to any form of sharing” and that the President “is the sole decision-maker concerning the deployment of nuclear forces and, more broadly, the doctrine and sizing of national capabilities.” The document emphasizes that this decision-making autonomy cannot be called into question, “including when implementing the European dimension of France’s deterrence strategy. While the interests of allies may be taken into account in the President’s decision-making process, that decision remains sovereign and is always based on an assessment of the Nation’s vital interests.” [Translation by the author.] However, the expectations of some partners may go beyond such loose assurances of being heard. For instance, Merz said on July 17 during a press conference after a meeting of the Franco-German Defense and Security Council that France and Germany are embarking now on a “new, common way” on deterrence. He described the work on a “joint doctrine” to involve discussions in the Nuclear Steering Group on the appropriate “mix of nuclear and conventional capabilities” to improve deterrence. [Translation by the author.] Still, differences between French nuclear priorities and those of its partners exist. Take nuclear arms control. NATO has historically paired initiatives to strengthen deterrence and defense with offers of engagement to Moscow. But Macron put out little hope for pursuing a similar dual-track approach, saying that “the field of rules has turned into a field of ruins.” He argued that because “the prevailing animosity does not inspire the confidence required to rebuild the norms of collective security,” France is “right to harden [its] position.” Unsurprisingly then, bilateral statements issued by Paris and its nuclear partners do not refer to arms control and only mention nuclear nonproliferation as a shared goal. Berlin and Paris merely state that they “will continue to comply with their obligations under international law including the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons” (NPT). France and the United Kingdom, in the Northwood declaration, reaffirm their “full support” for the NPT and for their obligations under the treaty. They promise to “coordinate ever more closely to uphold and reinforce the international non-proliferation architecture.” Even under the NPT, some of France’s non-nuclear partners have a level of ambition that goes beyond such generic support and is at odds with French nuclear policy. Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland, for example, are participants of the Non-proliferation and Disarmament Initiative, which has called on nuclear weapon states to improve the transparency of information related to their nuclear weapons. But in his speech, not only did Macron announce a nuclear weapons build-up, but he also reduced French nuclear transparency: “To put an end to any speculation, we will no longer release figures on our nuclear arsenal, as we have done in the past.” Will France’s non-nuclear partners be successful in urging Paris to reduce such discrepancies with their own policies? To be sure, they might be more successful if addressing such differences collectively, rather than in asymmetrical one-to-one dialogues. Alignment with NATO nuclear deterrence. In his nuclear speech, Macron was at pains to avoid any impression that his initiative could be seen as a competition to NATO’s nuclear sharing arrangements. Forward deterrence, he said, “is a distinct effort which has its own value and is perfectly complementary to NATO’s at both strategic and technical level.” Such separation may seem feasible and desirable from a French perspective. Paris, after all, is not ready to involve its non-nuclear partners in joint nuclear planning and restricts their participation to practical arrangements such as joint exercises or conventional support for nuclear strike missions. But things look different for non-nuclear partners. They would, for example, want to insist that France and NATO deconflict their nuclear targeting by making sure that the set of nuclear targets in respective operational plans does sit well together. Allies would also want to avoid a situation in which Paris is requesting support for one nuclear mission, while a separate request may come in from NATO, via the Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR). This concern is not abstract. On July 16, German fighter aircraft participated for the first time in a joint air activity in the context of the French concept of forward deterrence. The nuclear exercise involved two nuclear-capable French Rafale aircraft and two German Eurofighters from Nörvenich Air Force Base, as well as a French multirole tanker and transport Phenix aircraft for air-to-air refueling. The exercise took place ahead of the July 17 meetings of the Franco-German Defense and Security Council and the French-German Nuclear Steering Group. But non-nuclear NATO members only have a specific set of capabilities to provide such conventional support for nuclear missions, and they may not be able to put them on the table for NATO as well as possible French missions. The Northwood declaration adds another level of complexity because the United Kingdom has assigned all its nuclear weapons to NATO, meaning that SACEUR can request the employment of UK (but not of French) nuclear weapons. More difficulties for non-nuclear weapon states in aligning NATO nuclear sharing and forward deterrence may lie ahead. The United States is drawing down its conventional forces in Europe at the same time it is trying to compensate for the resulting commitment deficit by increasing reliance on NATO nuclear sharing. To that aim, Washington reportedly has been in talks with Poland and maybe other French partners to sell them additional dual-capable F-35 aircraft, which could be certified to carry US B61 nuclear gravity bombs. This shift away from conventional deterrence implies more emphasis on US nuclear weapons in Europe as warfighting tools. But this remains anathema to French nuclear thinking: Macron repeated in his March 2 speech the French nuclear mantra that “rejects the idea of flexible nuclear response.” In the Franco-German context, both countries have emphasized that forward deterrence will involve joint discussions “to manage escalation beneath the nuclear threshold and to develop the necessary conventional capabilities,” such as the “articulation of conventional, Deep Precision Strike and missile defence capabilities with nuclear deterrence.” For non-nuclear weapon states, this relationship between conventional and nuclear deterrence was always the crux of discussions within NATO. They feared either abandonment by their nuclear allies or, vice versa, entanglement in nuclear warfighting plans. It is therefore hard to imagine how debates on forward deterrence with France can be limited to conventional aspects of deterrence, without also involving discussions on nuclear doctrine. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwzr.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on 10 September 2025 before he was shot and killed by a gunman By Sakshi Venkatraman Published 5 hours ago Charlie Kirk's family has accused the Utah Valley University and state officials of "stunning failures and reckless decisions" that they say led to the conservative activist's 2025 assassination during a campus event. In a legal notice, lawyers for the family say Kirk's Turning Point USA event at the university campus was not properly secured or monitored, making him an easy target. Kirk, 31, was speaking to a crowd of thousands on the university campus, when he was shot and killed by a gunman positioned on a roof. The university said it was aware of the claim but did not comment further on the allegations, according to a statement shared with the BBC's US partner CBS News. "We are aware of the notice of claim. UVU addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes, " the university said in its statement. "Our focus remains on supporting our campus community." The legal notice was filed on 9 September, a day ahead of the one-year anniversary of Kirk's death, and is typically a precursor to a lawsuit. It names Utah Valley University, local police, the state of Utah, and other university officials as parties who were allegedly aware of the threats against Kirk and did not take steps to protect him. "Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie," the notice alleges. "Placing a politically controversial figure like Charlie Kirk in an outdoor event in the quad surrounded by tall buildings and other elevated observation platforms is accurately described as walking him into a fishbowl," it says. Kirk's family alleges the university failed to conduct a meaningful security assessment ahead of the event, failed to assign enough police officers, and did not have an ambulance available on site. The family also alleges the university ignored warnings about securing the rooftops surrounding the courtyard where Kirk was speaking. "The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk's close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," the family's attorney D Loren Washburn wrote in the court filing. Tyler Robinson, a 23-year-old man from Utah, who has been accused of shooting Kirk from a roof, is due to appear in court next month to hear the date of his trial. Robinson denies aggravated murder, a capital offence in the state, as well as six other charges. Prosecutors have called for the death penalty. https://www.hindustantimes.com/ht-explai.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spent less than eight hours in New York on Thursday. He flew there across the airspace of three countries that were bound by a treaty to arrest him, delivered a combative address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), and was due to fly home the same day. All the while he remained the subject of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant.Flight-tracking app Flightradar24 showed his plane crossing Greece, Italy and France. All three are parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that set up the Hague-based ICC and obliges its members to arrest suspects on their territory.France said on Thursday that allowing the flight broke no rule. In New York, mayor Zohran Mamdani, who had campaigned on the promise of arresting Netanyahu if he came to the American city, had already conceded he had no power to do so.In New YorkNetanyahu reached New York around 9am local time and was expected to fly back later in the day after his speech. Two Israeli officials told Reuters he would be in the city for less than eight hours, of which his speech at UNGA took up 40 minutes. As dozens of delegates walked out during the speech, Netanyahu called them "moral cowards" and described allegations of genocide in Gaza as "the biggest lie of the century".Mamdani, whom Netanyahu also attacked from the podium, responded in a statement, saying: “No lie can change the fact that he remains the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant alleging war crimes and crimes against humanity.”Also read: Which countries walked out of Netanyahu's UNGA speech? Israeli PM reacts as delegates leave in dozensThe ICC warrantThe case arises from Israel's war in Gaza, which began after Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel bombed Gaza, killing thousands.The ICC prosecutor opened an investigation into the ‘Situation in the State of Palestine in March 2021’ and said that the investigation extends to the escalation of hostilities since the Hamas attacks. The prosecutor filed applications for arrest warrants with Pre-Trial Chamber I on May 20, 2024.Pre-Trial Chamber I of the ICC issued the warrants for Netanyahu and his then defence minister Yoav Gallant on November 21, 2024, in a unanimous decision that also threw out two challenges brought by Israel. The court lists the offences as the war crimes of starvation as a method of warfare and of intentionally directing an attack against the civilian population, and the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution and other inhumane acts, covering a period from at least October 8, 2023, to at least May 20, 2024.The court also issued a warrant for Hamas's then military commander, Mohammed Deif. Judges ended the proceedings against him in February 2025 after prosecutors notified the court of Deif’s death.Netanyahu denies the ICC's claims. Israel rejects ICC’s jurisdiction, denies committing war crimes in Gaza and is contesting the warrants.How can ICC act against a leader whose country is not a member?Israel has never ratified the Rome Statute.But, in its November 2024 decision, Pre-Trial Chamber I held that Israel's consent was unnecessary because the court can exercise jurisdiction on the basis of Palestine's territorial jurisdiction.Palestine accepted the court's jurisdiction by a declaration lodged on January 1, 2015, and acceded to the statute the next day. In February 2021, a majority of the same chamber, in an earlier composition, ruled that this jurisdiction covers Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem.Israel appealed. In April 2025, the Appeals Chamber found that the lower chamber had not adequately dealt with Israel's argument that it was entitled to challenge jurisdiction, and sent the question back for a fresh ruling. The appeals judges dismissed as moot Israel's request to suspend the two warrants.Also read: ‘Biggest lie of the century’: Benjamin Netanyahu rejects Gaza genocide allegations in UNGA speechWho is supposed to arrest Netanyahu?Member states are. The ICC has no police force or enforcement arm of its own, and depends on governments to make arrests and transfer suspects to its detention centre in The Hague.Under the statute, member states must cooperate fully with the court, and the court may send an arrest request to any state "on the territory of which that person may be found".Parties to the statute include 125 countries. The United States and Israel are not among them. (India is not a member either.)But the warrant has left Netanyahu unable to travel to many countries, Reuters reported.Holding office also offers no protection under the treaty. Article 27 says official capacity as a head of state or government exempts no one from criminal responsibility, and that immunities attached to that office do not bar the court from exercising its jurisdiction.How did Netanyahu fly over France?France, a party to the statute, defended its decision to let the Israeli leader's plane cross its airspace. Foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux told reporters the clearance was "in full conformity with international law"."The Rome Statute does not impose any obligations regarding overflights of its territory by a state plane which has a passenger who is targeted by an arrest warrant," Confavreux said.A spokesperson for Italy's foreign ministry could not immediately say whether Israel had sought permission to overfly Italy, according to Reuters. Last year, media reported that Netanyahu took a circuitous route to New York that skirted several European countries, including France.The statute's arrest duty is framed around a person being found on a state's territory. Part 9 of the statute, which governs arrest and surrender, does not define territory or say whether an aircraft passing overhead meets that test. The ‘use of terms’ clause in that part defines only surrender and extradition.The only airspace provision in the treaty's chapter on arrest and surrender deals with a suspect who is already in custody and being flown to the court. It says no transit authorisation is needed if no landing is scheduled. If the plane makes an unscheduled landing, the state concerned may ask the court for a transit request and must hold the prisoner for up to 96 hours until the request is received.France's position rests on the gap that the treaty has no provision on a wanted person flying freely over a member state.Why could Netanyahu not be arrested at the UN?The United States has no obligation to the ICC. Under the statute, the court can only invite a non-member state to help, through an ad hoc arrangement or an agreement with that state. The ICC is not a United Nations body, although the two have a cooperation agreement.The Donald Trump administration has also moved against the ICC. The US under Trump has imposed financial sanctions and visa bans on the ICC staff and Trump has said the campaign against ICC is aimed at protecting Netanyahu.What if member countries don’t make an arrest?The court can name them and refer them onwards, and that is the extent of its power. Under Article 87(7), if a member state fails to cooperate and so prevents ICC from doing its work, the judges may record that finding and refer the matter to the Assembly of States Parties, the body of member governments.The judges have made such findings before, including in the case of Sudan's then president Omar al-Bashir. The two most recent cases involve states that hosted wanted leaders.Mongolia and Putin. In October 2024, a pre-trial chamber found that Mongolia had failed in its obligations by not arresting Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit, and restated that the immunity of heads of state is "not opposable before the ICC, and no waiver is required".Hungary and Netanyahu. Hungary argued a similar point on his behalf. It told the court that because Israel is not a party and had not waived Netanyahu's immunity, he was protected by state immunity, and Article 98(1) barred the court from asking Hungary to arrest him. In a finding dated July 24, 2025, Pre-Trial Chamber I nonetheless ruled that Hungary broke its obligations by not arresting Netanyahu while he was in the country from April 3 to 6, 2025, and referred the matter to the Assembly of States Parties.Hungary announced during that visit that it would leave the court. It later reversed course. It withdrew its notice of withdrawal with immediate effect, notifying the UN secretary-general on May 29, 2026.The attack on ICCTrump used his UNGA address on Tuesday to urge countries to quit the court, calling it "evil" and "a rogue institution". In July, US secretary of state Marco Rubio launched a campaign to dismantle the court "brick by brick, if necessary".So far only Naoero, the Pacific island nation formerly known as Nauru, has said this week it will withdraw. After Rubio's statement, Venezuela and Chad also announced plans to leave, according to Reuters.Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger announced their exits last year and have now filed formal notice.The presidency of the Assembly of States Parties has said that leaving does not free a state from obligations that arose while it was still a member.European governments have closed ranks behind the court. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc had "tools in our toolbox" to defend it, Reuters reported. Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten told the Assembly the court was "under attack".
